# How to use this guide

Remedial Mathematics is taken in Semester 1 by students who studied biology, not mathematics, in Class 12. It starts from the basics and builds up to the equations used in pharmacokinetics. Marks in this subject come from **working**, not from writing: read a section, then close the notes and redo every worked example on paper until you get the same answer without help. Then try the question bank.

**How the subject is examined.** In the PCI scheme, BP106RMT is a 2-credit theory subject (2 hours a week) marked as a **Non University Examination (NUE)**, so your own college sets and marks the paper. Marks: 15 internal (10 from a sessional exam of 1 hour, 5 from continuous assessment) + **35 end-semester (1.5 hours)** = 50. The PCI regulations print this pattern for a 35-mark paper, and the full mock paper in this app follows it. Confirm the exact pattern with your college.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Long answers — answer 1 of 2 | 1 × 10 = 10 |
| II | Short answers — answer 5 of 7 | 5 × 5 = 25 |
| | **Total** | **35** |

The question bank also has 2-mark very short questions, useful for the sessional exam and for papers that ask short definitions.

**How the units are arranged.** The five units follow the five syllabus units exactly (each about 6 teaching hours). Unit 4 joins two syllabus topics, analytical geometry and integration, because the syllabus puts them in the same unit.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — this type of problem appears in most papers; practise several versions until you can do them quickly.
- **Medium** — appears every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common question patterns, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Problems that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Partial fractions, logs, limits | Resolve into partial fractions (linear, repeated, quadratic factors); laws of logarithms; characteristic and mantissa; limits using (x^n − a^n)/(x − a) and sin θ/θ; continuity at a point |
| 2 Matrices | Inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix; solving three equations by matrix method and Cramer's rule; verifying Cayley–Hamilton and using it for A^−1; properties of determinants |
| 3 Differentiation | Product and quotient rule problems; successive derivatives; maxima and minima of a cubic |
| 4 Geometry and integration | Distance, slope, equation of a line (parallel/perpendicular); integration by substitution, partial fractions and by parts; definite integrals |
| 5 DE and Laplace | Order and degree; separable, homogeneous, linear and exact equations; Laplace transforms of standard functions; solving a DE by Laplace; first-order kinetics and IV infusion |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Write every step on its own line. Examiners give method marks even when the last number is wrong, but only if they can see the method.
2. Write the formula or rule you are using before substituting (for example "quotient rule: (vu′ − uv′)/v^2").
3. Check your answer whenever you can: put x = 0 into a partial fraction; multiply A by A^−1 to get I; put the solution back into the equations; differentiate an integral to get the integrand back.
4. Box the final answer and, for integrals, never forget "+ c".
5. In matrix questions, show |A| first. If |A| = 0, say the matrix is singular and has no inverse.
6. For maxima and minima, state the test (f′ = 0, sign of f″) and give both the point and the value.
7. Where a question says "application", add one pharmacy example: first-order kinetics (C = C0e^(−kt), t½ = 0.693/k), IV infusion, AUC = C0/k, Beer–Lambert calibration line, pH = −log[H+].
8. Learn the five standard tables in the revision sheet (logs laws, derivatives, integrals, Laplace pairs, DE methods); most marks depend on recalling them correctly.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only one evening, practise one full example of each of these: **partial fractions with a repeated factor**, **inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix**, **Cayley–Hamilton verification**, **maxima and minima of a cubic**, **integration by parts**, **a linear differential equation**, and **solving a differential equation by Laplace transform**. Together they cover most long answers.

**Partial fractions (Unit 1)**

| Denominator factor | Write |
| --- | --- |
| (x − a) | A/(x − a) |
| (x − a)^2 | A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)^2 |
| (x^2 + bx + c), no real factors | (Ax + B)/(x^2 + bx + c) |

Improper fraction → divide first. Find constants by putting x = roots, then compare coefficients. Check at x = 0.

**Logarithms (Unit 1)**

- log(mn) = log m + log n; log(m/n) = log m − log n; log m^n = n log m; log_a a = 1; log 1 = 0.
- ln x = 2.303 log x; log_a N = log N/log a.
- Characteristic: number > 1 → (digits before decimal − 1); 0 < number < 1 → −(zeros after decimal + 1). Mantissa always positive: log 0.0345 = 2̄.5378.
- pH = −log[H+]; pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]); k = (2.303/t) log(C0/C).

**Limits and continuity (Unit 1)**

- lim (x → a) (x^n − a^n)/(x − a) = n·a^(n − 1); lim (θ → 0) sin θ/θ = 1; lim (1 − cos x)/x^2 = 1/2.
- Try substitution first; on 0/0 factorise, rationalise or use a standard limit.
- Continuous at a: f(a) defined, LHL = RHL = f(a).

**Matrices (Unit 2)**

- AB needs columns of A = rows of B; AB ≠ BA; (AB)^T = B^T A^T; |AB| = |A||B|.
- Cofactor Cij = (−1)^(i + j) Mij; adj A = (cofactor matrix)^T; A^−1 = adj A/|A| (needs |A| ≠ 0).
- 2 × 2: [a b; c d]^−1 = (1/(ad − bc))[d −b; −c a].
- AX = B → X = A^−1B; Cramer: x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D.
- Characteristic equation |A − λI| = 0; 2 × 2: λ^2 − (trace)λ + |A| = 0. Cayley–Hamilton: A satisfies it.

**Derivatives (Unit 3)**

| f | f′ | f | f′ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| x^n | n x^(n − 1) | sin x | cos x |
| e^x | e^x | cos x | −sin x |
| a^x | a^x ln a | tan x | sec^2 x |
| ln x | 1/x | sec x | sec x tan x |
| √x | 1/(2√x) | cot x | −cosec^2 x |

Product uv′ + vu′; quotient (vu′ − uv′)/v^2; chain: × derivative of the inside. Max: f′ = 0, f″ < 0; min: f′ = 0, f″ > 0. tmax = ln(ka/k)/(ka − k).

**Geometry (Unit 4)**

- Distance √[(x2 − x1)^2 + (y2 − y1)^2]; slope (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1); ax + by + c = 0 → m = −a/b.
- Parallel m1 = m2; perpendicular m1m2 = −1; y = mx + c; y − y1 = m(x − x1).

**Integrals (Unit 4)**

| ∫ | Result | ∫ | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| x^n | x^(n + 1)/(n + 1) | sin x | −cos x |
| 1/x | ln\|x\| | cos x | sin x |
| e^(ax) | e^(ax)/a | sec^2 x | tan x |
| a^x | a^x/ln a | 1/(1 + x^2) | tan^−1 x |
| f′/f | ln\|f\| | 1/(x^2 − a^2) | (1/2a) ln\|(x − a)/(x + a)\| |

By parts: ∫uv dx = u∫v dx − ∫[u′∫v dx]dx, u chosen by ILATE. Definite: F(b) − F(a). AUC (IV bolus) = C0/k; trapezoid strip = (C1 + C2)/2 × Δt.

**Differential equations (Unit 5)**

| Type | Method |
| --- | --- |
| Separable | f(y)dy = g(x)dx, integrate both sides |
| Homogeneous | y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx |
| Linear dy/dx + Py = Q | IF = e^(∫P dx); y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + c |
| Exact M dx + N dy = 0 | ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x; ∫M dx + ∫(N terms without x) dy = c |

Kinetics: dC/dt = −kC → C = C0e^(−kt), t½ = 0.693/k; zero order C = C0 − k0t, t½ = C0/2k0; infusion X = (k0/k)(1 − e^(−kt)), Css = k0/CL.

**Laplace transform (Unit 5)**

| f(t) | F(s) | f(t) | F(s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1/s | sin at | a/(s^2 + a^2) |
| t^n | n!/s^(n + 1) | cos at | s/(s^2 + a^2) |
| e^(at) | 1/(s − a) | sinh at | a/(s^2 − a^2) |
| e^(−at) | 1/(s + a) | cosh at | s/(s^2 − a^2) |

L{f′} = sF − f(0); L{f″} = s^2F − s f(0) − f′(0); L{e^(at)f} = F(s − a). Oral one-compartment model: X = [ka F D/(ka − k)](e^(−kt) − e^(−ka·t)).

**Five checks before you hand in:** partial fractions recombine; A·A^−1 = I; solution satisfies the original equations; derivative of your integral gives the integrand; every indefinite integral ends with + c.

questions.answer:
1. Rules: the fraction must be proper; a linear factor (x − a) gives A/(x − a); a repeated factor (x − a)^2 gives A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)^2; a quadratic factor that cannot be factorised gives (Ax + B)/(quadratic).
2. (a) Form: (3x + 1)/((x − 1)^2 (x + 2)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 1)^2 + C/(x + 2).
3. Multiply by (x − 1)^2 (x + 2): 3x + 1 = A(x − 1)(x + 2) + B(x + 2) + C(x − 1)^2.
4. Put x = 1: 4 = 3B → B = 4/3. Put x = −2: −5 = 9C → C = −5/9.
5. Compare coefficients of x^2: 0 = A + C → A = 5/9.
6. Answer (a): 5/(9(x − 1)) + 4/(3(x − 1)^2) − 5/(9(x + 2)).
7. Check at x = 0: left = 1/2; right = −5/9 + 4/3 − 5/18 = (−10 + 24 − 5)/18 = 9/18 = 1/2 ✓.
8. (b) Form: x/((x + 1)(x^2 + 1)) = A/(x + 1) + (Bx + C)/(x^2 + 1), so x = A(x^2 + 1) + (Bx + C)(x + 1).
9. Put x = −1: −1 = 2A → A = −1/2. Coefficient of x^2: 0 = A + B → B = 1/2. Constant: 0 = A + C → C = 1/2. Coefficient of x: B + C = 1 ✓.
10. Answer (b): −1/(2(x + 1)) + (x + 1)/(2(x^2 + 1)).
11. Use: partial fractions are needed to integrate rational functions and to find inverse Laplace transforms in kinetics and pharmacokinetics.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: if a^x = N (a > 0, a ≠ 1), then x = log_a N.
2. Product law: let log_a m = x, log_a n = y, so m = a^x, n = a^y. mn = a^(x + y), hence log_a(mn) = x + y = log_a m + log_a n.
3. Quotient law: m/n = a^(x − y), hence log_a(m/n) = log_a m − log_a n.
4. Power law: m^p = (a^x)^p = a^(px), hence log_a m^p = p log_a m.
5. Also log_a a = 1, log_a 1 = 0, and change of base log_a N = log N/log a (ln x = 2.303 log x).
6. Characteristic = whole-number part of a common log; mantissa = decimal part, always positive (from tables).
7. Number > 1: characteristic = digits before decimal − 1. log 3456 = 3.5386 (characteristic 3).
8. Number between 0 and 1: characteristic = −(zeros after decimal + 1), written with a bar. log 0.0345 = 2̄.5378 = −1.4622.
9. Mantissa depends only on the digits: log 3.456 = 0.5386, log 345.6 = 2.5386.
10. Problem: k = (2.303/t) log(C0/C) = (2.303/40) × log(500/350) = (2.303/40) × 0.1549 = 0.00892 per day.
11. t½ = 0.693/k = 0.693/0.00892 = 77.7 days. Shelf life t90 = 0.105/k = 11.8 days.

questions.answer:
1. Theorem: every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation |A − λI| = 0.
2. |A − λI| = (3 − λ)[(1 − λ)^2 − 4] = (3 − λ)(λ^2 − 2λ − 3).
3. Characteristic equation: λ^3 − 5λ^2 + 3λ + 9 = 0 (trace 5, sum of diagonal minors 3 + 3 − 3 = 3, |A| = −9). Roots 3, 3, −1.
4. A^2 = [5 4 0; 4 5 0; 0 0 9]; A^3 = [13 14 0; 14 13 0; 0 0 27].
5. A^3 − 5A^2 + 3A + 9I: element (1,1) = 13 − 25 + 3 + 9 = 0; (1,2) = 14 − 20 + 6 = 0; (3,3) = 27 − 45 + 9 + 9 = 0; the others are 0 similarly, so the result is the null matrix. Theorem verified.
6. Multiply A^3 − 5A^2 + 3A + 9I = O by A^−1: A^2 − 5A + 3I + 9A^−1 = O.
7. A^−1 = −(A^2 − 5A + 3I)/9. A^2 − 5A + 3I = [5 − 5 + 3, 4 − 10, 0; 4 − 10, 3, 0; 0, 0, 9 − 15 + 3] = [3 −6 0; −6 3 0; 0 0 −3].
8. A^−1 = (1/3)[−1 2 0; 2 −1 0; 0 0 1].

# Unit 1: Partial fractions, logarithms, functions, limits and continuity

This unit gives you the basic tools that the rest of the course keeps using. Partial fractions come back in integration and in the Laplace transform; logarithms are needed for pH, half-life and every first-order equation; limits are the starting point of differentiation. Work every example with a pen as you read.

**How maths is written in these notes:** x^2 means "x squared", x^3 "x cubed", √x "square root of x", log x is the common log (base 10), ln x is the natural log (base e), and a/b means a divided by b. Brackets show what is on top and what is below: (3x + 5)/((x + 2)(x − 1)).

## 1.1 Polynomials and rational fractions

A **polynomial** in x is a sum of terms of the form a·x^n, where n is 0 or a positive whole number.

| Example | Degree (highest power) | Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7 | 0 | Constant |
| 3x − 2 | 1 | Linear |
| x^2 − 5x + 6 | 2 | Quadratic |
| 2x^3 + x − 1 | 3 | Cubic |

A **rational fraction** is one polynomial divided by another, P(x)/Q(x), with Q(x) not zero.

- **Proper fraction:** degree of top < degree of bottom. Example: (2x + 3)/(x^2 + x − 2).
- **Improper fraction:** degree of top ≥ degree of bottom. Example: (x^2 + 1)/(x^2 − 3x + 2). First divide (long division) to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction.

## 1.2 Partial fractions

Adding fractions joins them: 1/(x − 1) + 1/(x + 1) = 2x/(x^2 − 1). **Resolving into partial fractions** is the reverse: breaking one fraction into simpler ones. We need it to integrate rational functions and to find inverse Laplace transforms.

**Rules for the form of the partial fractions** (fraction must be proper first):

| Factor in the denominator | Partial fraction to write |
| --- | --- |
| Linear (x − a), not repeated | A/(x − a) |
| Repeated linear (x − a)^2 | A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)^2 |
| (x − a)^3 | A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)^2 + C/(x − a)^3 |
| Quadratic that cannot be factorised (x^2 + bx + c) | (Ax + B)/(x^2 + bx + c) |

**Method:** write the form, multiply both sides by the full denominator, then (1) put x equal to the roots of the linear factors to get constants quickly, and (2) compare coefficients of equal powers of x for the rest. Always check your answer at one more value of x.

### Example 1: two different linear factors

Resolve (3x + 5)/((x + 2)(x − 1)).

```text
(3x + 5)/((x + 2)(x − 1)) = A/(x + 2) + B/(x − 1)
Multiply by (x + 2)(x − 1):
  3x + 5 = A(x − 1) + B(x + 2)
Put x = 1:   8 = 3B      → B = 8/3
Put x = −2: −1 = −3A     → A = 1/3
Answer:
  1/(3(x + 2)) + 8/(3(x − 1))
Check at x = 0:
  left  = 5/(2 × −1) = −5/2
  right = 1/6 − 8/3 = 1/6 − 16/6 = −15/6 = −5/2 ✓
```

### Example 2: a repeated factor

Resolve (3x + 1)/((x − 1)^2 (x + 2)).

```text
= A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 1)^2 + C/(x + 2)
3x + 1 = A(x − 1)(x + 2) + B(x + 2) + C(x − 1)^2
x = 1:   4 = 3B    → B = 4/3
x = −2: −5 = 9C    → C = −5/9
Compare x^2 terms: 0 = A + C → A = 5/9
Answer:
  5/(9(x − 1)) + 4/(3(x − 1)^2) − 5/(9(x + 2))
Check x = 0: left = 1/(1 × 2) = 1/2
  right = −5/9 + 4/3 − 5/18
        = −10/18 + 24/18 − 5/18 = 9/18 = 1/2 ✓
```

### Example 3: a quadratic factor

Resolve x/((x + 1)(x^2 + 1)).

```text
= A/(x + 1) + (Bx + C)/(x^2 + 1)
x = A(x^2 + 1) + (Bx + C)(x + 1)
x = −1:  −1 = 2A        → A = −1/2
x^2:      0 = A + B     → B = 1/2
constant: 0 = A + C     → C = 1/2
x terms:  1 = B + C = 1 ✓
Answer: −1/(2(x + 1)) + (x + 1)/(2(x^2 + 1))
```

### Example 4: an improper fraction

Resolve (x^2 + 1)/(x^2 − 3x + 2).

```text
Divide first: (x^2 + 1) ÷ (x^2 − 3x + 2) = 1,
  remainder (x^2 + 1) − (x^2 − 3x + 2) = 3x − 1
So = 1 + (3x − 1)/((x − 1)(x − 2))
3x − 1 = A(x − 2) + B(x − 1)
x = 1: 2 = −A → A = −2
x = 2: 5 = B
Answer: 1 − 2/(x − 1) + 5/(x − 2)
Check x = 0: left = 1/2; right = 1 + 2 − 5/2 = 1/2 ✓
```

### Application in chemical kinetics and pharmacokinetics

**Second-order reaction with unequal concentrations.** For A + B → products with starting concentrations a and b, the rate is dx/dt = k(a − x)(b − x). To integrate, split the fraction:

```text
1/((a − x)(b − x)) = [1/(b − a)] × [1/(a − x) − 1/(b − x)]
Check: 1/(a − x) − 1/(b − x)
     = (b − x − a + x)/((a − x)(b − x))
     = (b − a)/((a − x)(b − x)) ✓
Integrating (Unit 4) and using x = 0 at t = 0 gives
  kt = [1/(b − a)] ln[ a(b − x) / (b(a − x)) ]
```

**Pharmacokinetics.** After an oral dose the amount in the body comes out (Unit 5) as a constant times 1/((s + ka)(s + k)). Partial fractions split it into 1/(s + k) and 1/(s + ka), which turn into e^(−kt) and e^(−ka·t). That is how the familiar curve of absorption followed by elimination is obtained.

## 1.3 Logarithms

**Definition:** if a^x = N (a > 0, a ≠ 1), then x = log_a N. The logarithm is the power to which the base must be raised to give the number.

| Exponential form | Log form |
| --- | --- |
| 10^2 = 100 | log 100 = 2 |
| 2^5 = 32 | log_2 32 = 5 |
| 10^−3 = 0.001 | log 0.001 = −3 |
| e^0 = 1 | ln 1 = 0 |

- **Common logarithm:** base 10, written log x. Used in pH and in log tables.
- **Natural logarithm:** base e (e ≈ 2.718), written ln x. Used in calculus and kinetics.
- **Change of base:** log_a N = log_b N / log_b a. In particular ln x = 2.303 log x.
- Log of zero or a negative number is not defined.

### Laws (theorems) of logarithms

| Law | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| Product | log(mn) = log m + log n |
| Quotient | log(m/n) = log m − log n |
| Power | log(m^n) = n log m |
| Base | log_a a = 1 |
| One | log_a 1 = 0 |
| Inverse | a^(log_a N) = N |

**Proof of the product law (asked often):** let log_a m = x and log_a n = y, so m = a^x and n = a^y. Then mn = a^x · a^y = a^(x + y), so log_a(mn) = x + y = log_a m + log_a n.

### Worked examples on the laws

Given log 2 = 0.3010 and log 3 = 0.4771:

```text
log 12  = log(2^2 × 3) = 2(0.3010) + 0.4771 = 1.0791
log 1.5 = log 3 − log 2 = 0.4771 − 0.3010 = 0.1761
log 72  = log(2^3 × 3^2) = 0.9030 + 0.9542 = 1.8572
log √27 = (3/2) log 3 = 0.7157
```

**Solve:** log(x + 2) + log(x − 1) = 1.

```text
log[(x + 2)(x − 1)] = 1 → (x + 2)(x − 1) = 10
x^2 + x − 12 = 0 → (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0
x = 3 or x = −4
x = −4 makes log(x − 1) the log of a negative
number, so reject it. Answer: x = 3
```

**Solve:** log_8 x = 2/3 → x = 8^(2/3) = (8^(1/3))^2 = 2^2 = 4.

### Characteristic and mantissa

A common log has two parts: the **characteristic** (whole-number part) and the **mantissa** (decimal part, always positive, read from tables).

| Number | Characteristic rule | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Greater than 1 | (number of digits before the decimal point) − 1 | 3456 → 3 |
| Between 0 and 1 | −(number of zeros just after the decimal point + 1) | 0.0345 → −2 |

The mantissa depends only on the digits, not on the decimal point: log 3.456 = 0.5386, so log 3456 = 3.5386 and log 345.6 = 2.5386.

A negative characteristic is written with a bar over it so the mantissa stays positive:

```text
log 0.0345 = 2̄.5378   (means −2 + 0.5378 = −1.4622)
log 0.000589 = 4̄.7701 (means −4 + 0.7701 = −3.2299)
```

**Antilogarithm** is the reverse: antilog 2.5386 = 345.6 (put the decimal point so that there are 3 digits before it).

### Application of logarithms to pharmaceutical problems

**pH.** pH = −log[H+].

```text
[H+] = 3.2 × 10^−4 M
pH = −(log 3.2 + log 10^−4) = −(0.5051 − 4)
   = 3.4949 ≈ 3.49

pH = 5.6 → [H+] = 10^−5.6 = 10^0.4 × 10^−6
   = 2.51 × 10^−6 M
```

**Buffer pH (Henderson–Hasselbalch).** pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). Acetic acid 0.1 M with sodium acetate 0.2 M, pKa 4.76: pH = 4.76 + log 2 = 4.76 + 0.301 = 5.06.

**First-order decomposition and half-life.** k = (2.303/t) log(C0/C), t½ = 0.693/k and shelf life t90 = 0.105/k.

```text
A drug solution falls from 500 to 350 units in 40 days.
k = (2.303/40) × log(500/350)
  = (2.303/40) × 0.1549 = 0.00892 per day
t½  = 0.693/0.00892 = 77.7 days
t90 = 0.105/0.00892 = 11.8 days
```

## 1.4 Functions

A **function** f from set A to set B is a rule that gives **each** element x of A **exactly one** element f(x) of B. A is the **domain**, the set of values f(x) actually takes is the **range**. If both are sets of real numbers, f is a **real valued function** of a real variable.

**Finding the domain:**

- f(x) = 1/(x − 2): bottom cannot be zero, so domain = all real numbers except 2.
- f(x) = √(x − 3): inside the root cannot be negative, so x ≥ 3.
- f(x) = log(x + 1): needs x + 1 > 0, so x > −1.

### Classification of real valued functions

| Type | Rule | Example / note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Constant | f(x) = c | f(x) = 5; graph is a horizontal line |
| Identity | f(x) = x | Line through origin at 45° |
| Polynomial | a0 + a1x + … + anx^n | x^2 − 5x + 6 |
| Rational | P(x)/Q(x) | (x + 1)/(x − 2) |
| Modulus | f(x) = \|x\| | x if x ≥ 0, −x if x < 0 |
| Signum | 1, 0, −1 for x > 0, = 0, < 0 | Shows the sign of x |
| Greatest integer | [x] | [2.7] = 2, [−1.2] = −2 |
| Exponential | a^x, e^x | First-order drug decline C0e^(−kt) |
| Logarithmic | log_a x | Inverse of the exponential |
| Trigonometric | sin x, cos x, tan x … | Periodic |

Other ways to classify:

- **Algebraic** (built from x by +, −, ×, ÷, roots) and **transcendental** (exponential, log, trigonometric).
- **Even:** f(−x) = f(x), e.g. x^2, cos x (graph symmetric about the y-axis). **Odd:** f(−x) = −f(x), e.g. x^3, sin x.
- **Explicit** y = f(x), and **implicit** f(x, y) = 0, e.g. x^2 + y^2 = 25.
- **One-one** (different x give different f(x)) and **onto** (every element of B is reached).

## 1.5 Limits

**Idea:** lim (x → a) f(x) = L means f(x) gets as close as we like to L when x is close enough to a (x itself need not equal a).

**ε–δ definition:** lim (x → a) f(x) = L if for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that |f(x) − L| < ε whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ.

**Example (prove with ε–δ):** lim (x → 2) (3x + 1) = 7.

```text
|f(x) − 7| = |3x + 1 − 7| = 3|x − 2|
We want 3|x − 2| < ε, i.e. |x − 2| < ε/3.
Choose δ = ε/3. Then 0 < |x − 2| < δ gives
|f(x) − 7| < 3(ε/3) = ε. Hence the limit is 7.
```

**Left and right limits:** the limit exists only if the left-hand limit (x → a−) and right-hand limit (x → a+) are equal. For f(x) = |x|/x at x = 0, LHL = −1 and RHL = +1, so the limit does not exist.

**Limit laws:** the limit of a sum, difference, product or quotient (bottom limit not zero) is the sum, difference, product or quotient of the limits.

### Two standard limits from the syllabus

```text
1)  lim (x → a) (x^n − a^n)/(x − a) = n·a^(n − 1)
2)  lim (θ → 0) sin θ / θ = 1   (θ in radians)
```

Consequences: lim (x → 0) tan x / x = 1 and lim (x → 0) (1 − cos x)/x^2 = 1/2.

### Worked examples

```text
(a) lim (x → 2) (x^2 − 4)/(x − 2)
    = lim (x + 2)(x − 2)/(x − 2) = 2 + 2 = 4

(b) lim (x → 3) (x^4 − 81)/(x − 3)
    = 4 × 3^3 = 108      (formula 1 with n = 4, a = 3)

(c) lim (x → a) (x^5 − a^5)/(x^3 − a^3)
    divide top and bottom by (x − a):
    = (5a^4)/(3a^2) = (5/3)a^2

(d) lim (x → 0) sin 5x / x
    = 5 × lim sin 5x / 5x = 5 × 1 = 5

(e) lim (x → 0) sin 3x / sin 2x
    = (3x/2x) × 1 = 3/2

(f) lim (x → 0) (1 − cos x)/x^2
    1 − cos x = 2 sin^2(x/2)
    = 2 sin^2(x/2)/x^2 = (1/2)[sin(x/2)/(x/2)]^2
    → 1/2

(g) lim (x → 0) (√(1 + x) − 1)/x
    multiply top and bottom by (√(1 + x) + 1):
    = x / [x(√(1 + x) + 1)] = 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2

(h) lim (x → ∞) (3x^2 + 2x)/(5x^2 − 1)
    divide by x^2: (3 + 2/x)/(5 − 1/x^2) → 3/5

(i) lim (x → 2) (x^3 − 9)/(x − 3)
    bottom is not zero at x = 2, so substitute:
    (8 − 9)/(2 − 3) = 1
```

Tip (i): always try direct substitution first. Only when you get 0/0 do you factorise, rationalise or use a standard limit.

## 1.6 Continuity

A function f is **continuous at x = a** if three things hold:

1. f(a) is defined.
2. lim (x → a) f(x) exists (LHL = RHL).
3. lim (x → a) f(x) = f(a).

If any one fails, f is **discontinuous** at a. Polynomials, e^x, sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere; a rational function is continuous except where its bottom is zero.

**Example:** f(x) = (x^2 − 1)/(x − 1) for x ≠ 1, and f(1) = 2.

```text
lim (x → 1) (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x − 1) = 2 = f(1)
→ continuous at x = 1.
If instead f(1) = 3, the limit (2) ≠ f(1),
→ discontinuous at x = 1.
```

**Example:** find k so that f(x) = kx + 1 (x ≤ 2) and 3x − 1 (x > 2) is continuous at x = 2.

```text
LHL = f(2) = 2k + 1; RHL = 3(2) − 1 = 5
2k + 1 = 5 → k = 2
```

## Remember

- Make the fraction proper before splitting; use A/(x − a) for linear, add B/(x − a)^2 for a repeated factor, (Ax + B)/(quadratic) for a quadratic factor.
- Find constants by putting x = roots, then compare coefficients; always check at x = 0.
- log(mn) = log m + log n, log(m/n) = log m − log n, log m^n = n log m; ln x = 2.303 log x.
- Characteristic: digits before decimal − 1 (number > 1); −(zeros after decimal + 1) for 0 < number < 1; mantissa is always positive.
- pH = −log[H+]; t½ = 0.693/k; k = (2.303/t) log(C0/C).
- A function gives each x exactly one value; check domain for division by zero, roots of negatives and logs.
- lim (x^n − a^n)/(x − a) = n·a^(n − 1); lim sin θ/θ = 1 (θ in radians).
- Continuous at a: f(a) defined, LHL = RHL, and limit = f(a).

# Unit 2: Matrices and determinants

Matrices are a neat way to store numbers in rows and columns and to solve several equations at once. In pharmacy they appear when two drugs in one mixture are found from two absorbance readings, and when the rate equations of multi-compartment models are written together. This unit is the most predictable part of the paper: inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix, solving three equations, Cramer's rule and the Cayley–Hamilton theorem come almost every year.

## 2.1 What a matrix is

A **matrix** is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns, written inside square brackets. A matrix with m rows and n columns has **order m × n**. The element in row i and column j is written aij.

```text
A = [ 2  −1   4 ]      order 2 × 3
    [ 0   3   5 ]      a12 = −1, a23 = 5
```

## 2.2 Types of matrices

| Type | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Row matrix | One row | [1 4 7] |
| Column matrix | One column | 3 × 1 |
| Square matrix | Rows = columns | 2 × 2, 3 × 3 |
| Rectangular | Rows ≠ columns | 2 × 3 |
| Null (zero) matrix O | All elements 0 | [0 0; 0 0] |
| Diagonal matrix | Square; all off-diagonal elements 0 | diag(2, 5, 1) |
| Scalar matrix | Diagonal with all diagonal elements equal | diag(4, 4, 4) |
| Identity (unit) matrix I | Diagonal elements 1, rest 0 | I2, I3 |
| Upper triangular | All elements below the diagonal 0 | — |
| Lower triangular | All elements above the diagonal 0 | — |
| Symmetric | A^T = A (aij = aji) | — |
| Skew-symmetric | A^T = −A (diagonal all 0) | — |
| Singular | Square, \|A\| = 0 | — |
| Non-singular | Square, \|A\| ≠ 0 | — |

```text
I3 = [ 1 0 0 ]   symmetric  [ 1 2 3 ]   skew  [  0  2 −3 ]
     [ 0 1 0 ]              [ 2 4 5 ]         [ −2  0  4 ]
     [ 0 0 1 ]              [ 3 5 6 ]         [  3 −4  0 ]
```

The **principal (leading) diagonal** runs from top-left to bottom-right. Its sum is the **trace**.

## 2.3 Operations on matrices

**Equality:** same order and every element equal.

**Addition and subtraction:** only for matrices of the same order; add or subtract element by element. A + B = B + A.

**Scalar multiplication:** multiply every element by the number k.

**Multiplication AB:** possible only when the number of **columns of A = rows of B**. The element in row i, column j of AB = (row i of A) · (column j of B): multiply pair by pair and add. If A is m × n and B is n × p, AB is m × p.

```text
A = [ 1 2 ]   B = [ 2 0 ]
    [ 3 4 ]       [ 1 3 ]

AB: row1·col1 = 1×2 + 2×1 = 4
    row1·col2 = 1×0 + 2×3 = 6
    row2·col1 = 3×2 + 4×1 = 10
    row2·col2 = 3×0 + 4×3 = 12
AB = [  4  6 ]       BA = [  2  4 ]
     [ 10 12 ]            [ 10 14 ]
```

So **AB ≠ BA** in general (matrix multiplication is not commutative). It is associative, A(BC) = (AB)C, and distributive, A(B + C) = AB + AC. A·I = I·A = A.

## 2.4 Transpose

The **transpose** A^T (or A′) is obtained by turning rows into columns.

```text
A = [ 1 2 3 ]      A^T = [ 1 4 ]
    [ 4 5 6 ]            [ 2 5 ]
                         [ 3 6 ]
```

Properties: (A^T)^T = A; (A + B)^T = A^T + B^T; (kA)^T = kA^T; **(AB)^T = B^T A^T** (order reverses).

## 2.5 Determinants

Every square matrix has a single number called its **determinant**, written |A| or det A.

```text
2 × 2:  | a b |  = ad − bc
        | c d |

3 × 3 (expand along row 1):
| a1 b1 c1 |
| a2 b2 c2 | = a1(b2c3 − b3c2) − b1(a2c3 − a3c2)
| a3 b3 c3 |        + c1(a2b3 − a3b2)
```

Signs used in expansion follow the pattern:

```text
[ + − + ]
[ − + − ]
[ + − + ]
```

**Example:** solve for x.

```text
|  2  3  4 |
| −4  x −8 | = 0
|  5  6  7 |
2(7x − (−8)(6)) − 3((−4)(7) − (−8)(5))
   + 4((−4)(6) − 5x) = 0
2(7x + 48) − 3(−28 + 40) + 4(−24 − 5x) = 0
14x + 96 − 36 − 96 − 20x = 0
−6x − 36 = 0 → x = −6
Check: with x = −6, row 2 = −2 × row 1,
so the determinant is 0 ✓
```

### Properties of determinants

1. |A^T| = |A| (rows and columns can be swapped).
2. Swapping two rows (or columns) changes the sign.
3. Two identical rows (or columns) → determinant = 0.
4. Multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k; so a common factor of a row can be taken outside.
5. Adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the determinant unchanged.
6. A row of zeros → determinant = 0.
7. Determinant of a triangular or diagonal matrix = product of the diagonal elements.
8. **Product of determinants:** |AB| = |A| × |B|.

```text
Using A and B from 2.3:
|A| = 4 − 6 = −2,  |B| = 6 − 0 = 6
|AB| = 4×12 − 6×10 = −12 = (−2)(6) ✓
```

**Example using properties:** show that the determinant with rows (1, a, b + c), (1, b, c + a), (1, c, a + b) is zero.

```text
Add column 2 to column 3: column 3 becomes
(a + b + c) in every row = (a + b + c)(1, 1, 1).
Take (a + b + c) out: column 3 = column 1,
so the determinant = 0.
```

## 2.6 Minors and cofactors

- **Minor Mij** of element aij: the determinant left after deleting row i and column j.
- **Cofactor Cij** = (−1)^(i + j) Mij, i.e. the minor with the sign from the + − pattern.
- A determinant = sum of (elements of any row) × (their cofactors).

## 2.7 Adjoint, singular and non-singular matrices, inverse

- **Adjoint (adjugate) adj A** = transpose of the matrix of cofactors.
- A·(adj A) = (adj A)·A = |A| I.
- **Singular** if |A| = 0: no inverse. **Non-singular** if |A| ≠ 0: inverse exists.
- **Inverse:** A^−1 = (adj A)/|A|, and A·A^−1 = A^−1·A = I.
- 2 × 2 shortcut: for A = [a b; c d], A^−1 = (1/(ad − bc)) [d −b; −c a] (swap the diagonal, change signs of the other two).

### Example: inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix

```text
A = [ 1 0 −1 ]
    [ 1 2  1 ]
    [ 2 2  3 ]

Step 1: |A| = 1(2·3 − 1·2) − 0 + (−1)(1·2 − 2·2)
            = 1(4) − 1(−2) = 6   (≠ 0, inverse exists)

Step 2: cofactors
C11 = +(6 − 2)        = 4
C12 = −(3 − 2)        = −1
C13 = +(2 − 4)        = −2
C21 = −(0·3 − (−1)·2) = −2
C22 = +(3 − (−2))     = 5
C23 = −(2 − 0)        = −2
C31 = +(0·1 − (−1)·2) = 2
C32 = −(1 − (−1))     = −2
C33 = +(2 − 0)        = 2

Step 3: adj A = transpose of cofactor matrix
adj A = [  4 −2  2 ]
        [ −1  5 −2 ]
        [ −2 −2  2 ]

Step 4: A^−1 = (1/6) [  4 −2  2 ]
                     [ −1  5 −2 ]
                     [ −2 −2  2 ]

Check: row 1 of A × column 1 of adj A
       = 4 + 0 + 2 = 6; row 1 × column 2
       = −2 + 0 + 2 = 0 ... A·adj A = 6I ✓
```

## 2.8 Solving linear equations by the matrix method

Write the equations as **AX = B**. If |A| ≠ 0, the unique solution is **X = A^−1 B**.

**Consistency:** |A| ≠ 0 → one unique solution. |A| = 0 and (adj A)B ≠ O → no solution (inconsistent). |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = O → infinitely many solutions or none (check further).

### Example

Solve x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2, 2x + y − z = 1.

```text
A = [ 1  1  1 ]   X = [ x ]   B = [ 6 ]
    [ 1 −1  1 ]       [ y ]       [ 2 ]
    [ 2  1 −1 ]       [ z ]       [ 1 ]

|A| = 1(1 − 1) − 1(−1 − 2) + 1(1 + 2) = 0 + 3 + 3 = 6

Cofactors:
C11 = 0,  C12 = 3,  C13 = 3
C21 = 2,  C22 = −3, C23 = 1
C31 = 2,  C32 = 0,  C33 = −2

adj A = [ 0  2  2 ]
        [ 3 −3  0 ]
        [ 3  1 −2 ]

X = (1/6) adj A · B
x = (0×6 + 2×2 + 2×1)/6  = 6/6  = 1
y = (3×6 − 3×2 + 0×1)/6  = 12/6 = 2
z = (3×6 + 1×2 − 2×1)/6  = 18/6 = 3
Check in eq 3: 2 + 2 − 3 = 1 ✓
```

## 2.9 Cramer's rule

For AX = B with D = |A| ≠ 0: x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D, where Dx is D with the x-column replaced by the constants B (similarly Dy, Dz).

**Two equations:** 2x + 3y = 13, 3x − y = 3.

```text
D  = | 2  3 | = −2 − 9 = −11
     | 3 −1 |
Dx = | 13  3 | = −13 − 9 = −22  → x = 2
     |  3 −1 |
Dy = | 2 13 | = 6 − 39 = −33    → y = 3
     | 3  3 |
```

**Three equations** (same system as 2.8):

```text
D  = 6
Dx = | 6  1  1 |
     | 2 −1  1 | = 6(0) − 1(−3) + 1(3) = 6   → x = 1
     | 1  1 −1 |
Dy = | 1 6  1 |
     | 1 2  1 | = 1(−3) − 6(−3) + 1(−3) = 12 → y = 2
     | 2 1 −1 |
Dz = | 1  1 6 |
     | 1 −1 2 | = 1(−3) − 1(−3) + 6(3) = 18  → z = 3
     | 2  1 1 |
```

If D = 0, Cramer's rule cannot be used.

## 2.10 Characteristic equation, roots and Cayley–Hamilton theorem

For a square matrix A, **|A − λI| = 0** is the **characteristic equation**. Its roots λ are the **characteristic roots** (eigenvalues).

For a 2 × 2 matrix: λ^2 − (trace)λ + |A| = 0.
For a 3 × 3 matrix: λ^3 − (trace)λ^2 + (sum of the minors of the diagonal elements)λ − |A| = 0.

Useful facts: sum of roots = trace; product of roots = |A|; the roots of a triangular matrix are its diagonal elements.

**Cayley–Hamilton theorem:** every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. If λ^2 − 4λ + 3 = 0 is the characteristic equation, then A^2 − 4A + 3I = O.

### Example (2 × 2): verify and find the inverse

```text
A = [ 2 1 ]   trace = 4, |A| = 3
    [ 1 2 ]
Characteristic equation: λ^2 − 4λ + 3 = 0
Roots: (λ − 1)(λ − 3) = 0 → λ = 1, 3

A^2 = [ 5 4 ]   4A = [ 8 4 ]   3I = [ 3 0 ]
      [ 4 5 ]        [ 4 8 ]        [ 0 3 ]
A^2 − 4A + 3I = [ 0 0 ] = O  ✓ (theorem verified)
                [ 0 0 ]

Inverse: multiply A^2 − 4A + 3I = O by A^−1:
A − 4I + 3A^−1 = O → A^−1 = (4I − A)/3
A^−1 = (1/3) [  2 −1 ]
             [ −1  2 ]
```

### Example (3 × 3)

```text
A = [ 1 2 0 ]
    [ 2 1 0 ]
    [ 0 0 3 ]
|A − λI| = (3 − λ)[(1 − λ)^2 − 4]
         = (3 − λ)(λ^2 − 2λ − 3)
Characteristic equation:
  λ^3 − 5λ^2 + 3λ + 9 = 0  → roots 3, 3, −1

A^2 = [ 5 4 0 ]    A^3 = [ 13 14  0 ]
      [ 4 5 0 ]          [ 14 13  0 ]
      [ 0 0 9 ]          [  0  0 27 ]
A^3 − 5A^2 + 3A + 9I:
 (1,1): 13 − 25 + 3 + 9 = 0
 (1,2): 14 − 20 + 6     = 0
 (3,3): 27 − 45 + 9 + 9 = 0  ... all zero ✓

A^−1 = −(A^2 − 5A + 3I)/9
     = (1/3) [ −1  2 0 ]
             [  2 −1 0 ]
             [  0  0 1 ]
```

## 2.11 Applications of matrices in pharmacy

**1. Two drugs in one mixture (simultaneous equation method).** Absorbance is additive: at each wavelength A = a1·C1 + a2·C2. Two readings give two equations, solved by matrices or Cramer's rule.

```text
Absorptivities (per µg/ml): drug X 0.05 and 0.01,
drug Y 0.02 and 0.04 at λ1 and λ2.
Readings: 0.60 at λ1, 0.30 at λ2.
0.05x + 0.02y = 0.60
0.01x + 0.04y = 0.30
D  = 0.05×0.04 − 0.02×0.01 = 0.0018
Dx = 0.60×0.04 − 0.02×0.30 = 0.018  → x = 10 µg/ml
Dy = 0.05×0.30 − 0.60×0.01 = 0.009  → y = 5 µg/ml
```

**2. Pharmacokinetic compartment models.** In a two-compartment model the rates of change of drug in the central and peripheral compartments are linked equations. Writing them as one matrix equation dX/dt = K·X, with K the matrix of rate constants, lets them be solved together; the characteristic roots of K give the two exponents (α and β) of the plasma concentration curve.

**3. Other uses:** fitting straight lines to experimental data (least squares in matrix form), storing formula batches (ingredients × products) and multiplying by unit costs to cost a production plan.

## Remember

- Order m × n; AB exists only if columns of A = rows of B; AB ≠ BA in general.
- (AB)^T = B^T A^T; |AB| = |A||B|; |A^T| = |A|.
- Cofactor = (−1)^(i + j) × minor; adj A = transpose of cofactor matrix.
- A^−1 = adj A / |A|; exists only if |A| ≠ 0.
- AX = B → X = A^−1 B; Cramer: x = Dx/D.
- Characteristic equation |A − λI| = 0; 2 × 2: λ^2 − (trace)λ + |A| = 0.
- Cayley–Hamilton: A satisfies its own characteristic equation; use it to find A^−1 and powers of A.
- Always check: A·A^−1 = I, and put the solution back into one original equation.

# Unit 3: Calculus — differentiation, maxima and minima

Differentiation measures **how fast one quantity changes when another changes**. In pharmacy the rate at which a drug's concentration falls, the rate of a reaction and the time of the highest blood level are all derivatives. The syllabus asks for the rules without proof; what the examiner wants is correct, neat working.

Notation: dy/dx (or y′, f′(x)) is the derivative of y with respect to x. d²y/dx² (or y″) is the second derivative.

## 3.1 Derivative of a function

If y = f(x) and x changes by a small amount h, y changes by f(x + h) − f(x). The average rate is [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. Its limit as h → 0 is the **derivative**:

```text
dy/dx = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h
```

This is called differentiation **from first principles**. Geometrically, dy/dx is the **slope of the tangent** to the curve y = f(x) at the point x.

**Example (first principles):** y = x^2.

```text
f(x + h) − f(x) = (x + h)^2 − x^2 = 2xh + h^2
divide by h: 2x + h
limit as h → 0: 2x
So d/dx (x^2) = 2x
```

## 3.2 Standard derivatives (learn by heart)

| Function | Derivative |
| --- | --- |
| c (constant) | 0 |
| x^n (n any rational number) | n·x^(n − 1) |
| √x | 1/(2√x) |
| 1/x | −1/x^2 |
| e^x | e^x |
| a^x | a^x · ln a |
| ln x (log_e x) | 1/x |
| log_a x | 1/(x ln a) |
| sin x | cos x |
| cos x | −sin x |
| tan x | sec^2 x |
| cot x | −cosec^2 x |
| sec x | sec x · tan x |
| cosec x | −cosec x · cot x |

## 3.3 Rules of differentiation

| Rule | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Constant times a function | d/dx [c·f] = c·f′ |
| Sum or difference | d/dx [u ± v] = u′ ± v′ |
| Product (uv rule) | d/dx [uv] = u·v′ + v·u′ |
| Quotient (u/v rule) | d/dx [u/v] = (v·u′ − u·v′)/v^2 |
| Function of a function (chain) | dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx) |

Memory line for the quotient rule: "bottom times derivative of top, minus top times derivative of bottom, all over bottom squared".

### Worked examples: basic rules

```text
(1) y = 3x^4 − 5x^2 + 7x − 2
    dy/dx = 12x^3 − 10x + 7

(2) y = √x + 1/x = x^(1/2) + x^(−1)
    dy/dx = (1/2)x^(−1/2) − x^(−2)
          = 1/(2√x) − 1/x^2

(3) y = 5e^x + 3 ln x − 2^x
    dy/dx = 5e^x + 3/x − 2^x ln 2

(4) y = 4 sin x − 3 cos x + tan x
    dy/dx = 4 cos x + 3 sin x + sec^2 x
```

### Worked examples: product rule

```text
(5) y = x^2 sin x
    u = x^2, v = sin x
    dy/dx = x^2 cos x + sin x · 2x
          = x^2 cos x + 2x sin x

(6) y = x^4 · e^x · ln x   (three factors)
    dy/dx = 4x^3 e^x ln x + x^4 e^x ln x + x^4 e^x (1/x)
          = x^3 e^x (4 ln x + x ln x + 1)

(7) y = e^x ln x
    dy/dx = e^x (1/x) + ln x · e^x = e^x (1/x + ln x)
```

For three factors, differentiate one at a time and keep the other two: (uvw)′ = u′vw + uv′w + uvw′.

### Worked examples: quotient rule

```text
(8) y = (x^2 + 1)/(x − 1)
    u = x^2 + 1, u′ = 2x; v = x − 1, v′ = 1
    dy/dx = [(x − 1)(2x) − (x^2 + 1)(1)]/(x − 1)^2
          = (2x^2 − 2x − x^2 − 1)/(x − 1)^2
          = (x^2 − 2x − 1)/(x − 1)^2

(9) y = sin x/(1 + cos x)
    dy/dx = [(1 + cos x)cos x − sin x(−sin x)]/(1 + cos x)^2
          = (cos x + cos^2 x + sin^2 x)/(1 + cos x)^2
          = (1 + cos x)/(1 + cos x)^2 = 1/(1 + cos x)

(10) y = ln x / x
    dy/dx = [x(1/x) − ln x(1)]/x^2 = (1 − ln x)/x^2
```

### Worked examples: chain rule

```text
(11) y = (2x + 3)^5
     dy/dx = 5(2x + 3)^4 × 2 = 10(2x + 3)^4

(12) y = e^(−kt)      (differentiate with respect to t)
     dy/dt = e^(−kt) × (−k) = −k e^(−kt)

(13) y = sin(x^2)
     dy/dx = cos(x^2) × 2x = 2x cos(x^2)

(14) y = ln(x^2 + 1)
     dy/dx = 2x/(x^2 + 1)
```

## 3.4 Successive differentiation

Differentiating again gives the second derivative d²y/dx², then the third d³y/dx³, and so on.

```text
(15) y = x^3 + e^(2x)
     y′  = 3x^2 + 2e^(2x)
     y″  = 6x + 4e^(2x)
     y‴  = 6 + 8e^(2x)

(16) y = e^(ax): nth derivative = a^n e^(ax)

(17) y = sin 2x. Show y″ + 4y = 0.
     y′ = 2 cos 2x;  y″ = −4 sin 2x = −4y
     so y″ + 4y = 0 ✓

(18) y = A e^(mx) + B e^(−mx). Show y″ = m^2 y.
     y′ = mA e^(mx) − mB e^(−mx)
     y″ = m^2 A e^(mx) + m^2 B e^(−mx) = m^2 y ✓
```

Physical meaning: if s is distance and t time, ds/dt is velocity and d²s/dt² is acceleration.

## 3.5 Maxima and minima

At a highest point (**maximum**) or lowest point (**minimum**) of a smooth curve, the tangent is horizontal, so dy/dx = 0. Such points are **stationary (critical) points**.

```text
        max
        __
       /  \          dy/dx = 0 at both turning points
      /    \     /   left of max: rising (dy/dx > 0)
     /      \__ /    left of min: falling (dy/dx < 0)
               min
```

**Conditions (second-derivative test):**

| At x = a | Result |
| --- | --- |
| f′(a) = 0 and f″(a) < 0 | Maximum at a |
| f′(a) = 0 and f″(a) > 0 | Minimum at a |
| f′(a) = 0 and f″(a) = 0 | Test fails; check the sign of f′ on both sides |

**Steps:** (1) find f′(x); (2) solve f′(x) = 0; (3) find f″(x) at each root; (4) decide max or min; (5) put x back into f(x) for the maximum or minimum value.

### Example 1

Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x) = 2x^3 − 15x^2 + 36x + 10.

```text
f′(x) = 6x^2 − 30x + 36 = 6(x^2 − 5x + 6)
      = 6(x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 → x = 2 or 3
f″(x) = 12x − 30
x = 2: f″ = −6 < 0 → maximum
       f(2) = 16 − 60 + 72 + 10 = 38
x = 3: f″ = 6 > 0 → minimum
       f(3) = 54 − 135 + 108 + 10 = 37
Maximum value 38 (at x = 2);
minimum value 37 (at x = 3).
```

### Example 2

f(x) = x^3 − 3x^2 − 9x + 5.

```text
f′(x) = 3x^2 − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1) = 0
x = 3 or −1;  f″(x) = 6x − 6
x = −1: f″ = −12 → maximum, f(−1) = −1 − 3 + 9 + 5 = 10
x = 3:  f″ = 12  → minimum, f(3) = 27 − 27 − 27 + 5 = −22
```

### Example 3: when there is no maximum or minimum

f(x) = x^3/3 − 10x^2 + 300x.

```text
f′(x) = x^2 − 20x + 300
f′ = 0 → discriminant = 20^2 − 4(1)(300)
                      = 400 − 1200 = −800 < 0
No real roots. Also f′(x) = (x − 10)^2 + 200 > 0
for every x, so f is always increasing:
it has no maximum and no minimum.
```

Learn this trap: when f′(x) = 0 has no real roots, say clearly "no stationary point, so no maximum or minimum".

### Example 4: a word problem

Of all rectangles with perimeter 40 cm, which has the largest area?

```text
Sides x and (20 − x).  A = x(20 − x) = 20x − x^2
dA/dx = 20 − 2x = 0 → x = 10
d²A/dx² = −2 < 0 → maximum
Sides 10 cm and 10 cm (a square), area 100 cm^2.
```

## 3.6 Applications in pharmacy

**1. Rate of elimination.** For first-order elimination C = C0 e^(−kt):

```text
dC/dt = −k C0 e^(−kt) = −kC
The rate of fall is proportional to the
concentration present (first-order process).
```

**2. Time of peak plasma concentration (tmax) after an oral dose.** In a one-compartment model with first-order absorption, C = A(e^(−kt) − e^(−ka·t)), where ka is the absorption rate constant and k the elimination rate constant.

```text
dC/dt = A(−k e^(−kt) + ka e^(−ka·t)) = 0
ka e^(−ka·t) = k e^(−kt)
ka/k = e^((ka − k)t)
tmax = ln(ka/k) / (ka − k)

Example: ka = 1.0 per h, k = 0.2 per h
tmax = ln 5 / 0.8 = 1.609/0.8 = 2.01 h
```

**3. Rates of reaction.** In kinetics, the rate of a reaction is −d[A]/dt; the order of reaction describes how this derivative depends on concentration (zero, first or second order).

**4. Other uses:** sensitivity of a response to a small change in dose; finding the best (optimum) value of a formulation or process variable, such as the concentration that gives the highest response.

## Remember

- dy/dx = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h = slope of the tangent.
- d/dx x^n = n x^(n − 1); e^x → e^x; a^x → a^x ln a; ln x → 1/x.
- sin → cos; cos → −sin; tan → sec^2; cot → −cosec^2; sec → sec tan; cosec → −cosec cot.
- Product: uv′ + vu′; quotient: (vu′ − uv′)/v^2; chain: multiply by the derivative of the inside.
- Maximum: f′ = 0, f″ < 0; minimum: f′ = 0, f″ > 0. If f′ = 0 has no real roots, there is no max or min.
- First-order elimination: dC/dt = −kC; tmax = ln(ka/k)/(ka − k).

# Unit 4: Analytical geometry and integration

This unit has two parts. **Analytical (coordinate) geometry** describes points and straight lines with numbers; every calibration curve and every log-concentration-versus-time plot you draw in the lab is a straight line. **Integration** is the reverse of differentiation and is used to find areas, such as the area under a blood-level curve (AUC).

## Part A: Analytical geometry

## 4.1 Coordinates and their signs

Two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and the y-axis, meet at the **origin** O(0, 0). A point is written P(x, y): x is the **abscissa** (distance from the y-axis) and y the **ordinate** (distance from the x-axis).

```text
             y
   II (−, +) |  I (+, +)
             |
 ------------O------------ x
             |
  III (−, −) |  IV (+, −)
```

| Quadrant | Sign of x | Sign of y | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | + | + | (3, 2) |
| II | − | + | (−3, 2) |
| III | − | − | (−3, −2) |
| IV | + | − | (3, −2) |

Points on the x-axis have y = 0; points on the y-axis have x = 0.

## 4.2 Distance formula

The distance between P(x1, y1) and Q(x2, y2) is

```text
PQ = √[(x2 − x1)^2 + (y2 − y1)^2]
Distance of P from the origin = √(x1^2 + y1^2)
```

It comes from Pythagoras' theorem: the horizontal gap and vertical gap form the two shorter sides of a right triangle.

**Examples:**

```text
(a) A(1, 2), B(4, 6):
    AB = √(3^2 + 4^2) = √25 = 5

(b) Show (0, 0), (3, 0), (3, 4) form a right triangle.
    sides: 3, 4 and √(9 + 16) = 5
    3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2 → right angle at (3, 0) ✓

(c) Find k if the distance between (k, 2) and (1, 5) is 5.
    (k − 1)^2 + 9 = 25 → (k − 1)^2 = 16
    k − 1 = ±4 → k = 5 or −3
```

## 4.3 Slope (gradient) of a straight line

If a line makes an angle θ with the positive x-axis, its **slope** m = tan θ.

```text
Slope of the line through (x1, y1) and (x2, y2):
   m = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1)
```

| Line | Slope |
| --- | --- |
| Rising left to right | positive |
| Falling left to right | negative |
| Parallel to x-axis | 0 |
| Parallel to y-axis | not defined |
| Line ax + by + c = 0 | m = −a/b |

**Parallel lines** have equal slopes: m1 = m2.
**Perpendicular lines** have slopes whose product is −1: m1 × m2 = −1.

**Examples:**

```text
(a) Slope through (2, 3) and (6, 11): (11 − 3)/(6 − 2) = 2

(b) Are (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 5) collinear?
    slope AB = 2/1 = 2, slope BC = 2/1 = 2
    equal slopes and a common point → collinear ✓

(c) 2x − y + 3 = 0 has m = 2;
    x + 2y − 4 = 0 has m = −1/2;
    product = −1 → the lines are perpendicular
```

## 4.4 Equations of a straight line

| Form | Equation |
| --- | --- |
| Slope–intercept | y = mx + c (c = intercept on the y-axis) |
| Point–slope | y − y1 = m(x − x1) |
| Two-point | (y − y1)/(y2 − y1) = (x − x1)/(x2 − x1) |
| General | ax + by + c = 0 |

**Examples:**

```text
(a) Slope 3, y-intercept −2:  y = 3x − 2

(b) Slope and intercept of 2x + 3y − 6 = 0:
    3y = −2x + 6 → y = (−2/3)x + 2
    m = −2/3, c = 2

(c) Line through (−2, 0) perpendicular to 4x − 3y = 2:
    slope of given line = 4/3
    required slope = −3/4
    y − 0 = (−3/4)(x + 2)
    4y = −3x − 6 → 3x + 4y + 6 = 0

(d) Line through (1, 2) parallel to y = 5x + 7:
    m = 5 → y − 2 = 5(x − 1) → y = 5x − 3
```

## 4.5 Straight lines in pharmacy

**Calibration curve (Beer–Lambert law).** A = εbc, so absorbance against concentration is a straight line through the origin with slope εb.

```text
Standards: 2 µg/ml → A = 0.10; 6 µg/ml → A = 0.30
slope = (0.30 − 0.10)/(6 − 2) = 0.05 per µg/ml
intercept: 0.10 = 0.05(2) + c → c = 0
Unknown with A = 0.42: c = 0.42/0.05 = 8.4 µg/ml
```

**First-order kinetics.** log C = log C0 − kt/2.303 is the line y = mx + c with y = log C, x = t, slope m = −k/2.303 and intercept log C0. If the slope is −0.0434 per hour, k = 0.0434 × 2.303 = 0.100 per hour and t½ = 0.693/0.100 = 6.93 h.

**Zero-order kinetics.** C = C0 − k0·t is a straight line with slope −k0.

## Part B: Integration

## 4.6 Meaning of integration

If d/dx F(x) = f(x), then F(x) is an **integral (antiderivative)** of f(x):

```text
∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + c
```

The **constant of integration c** is added because the derivative of a constant is zero. ∫ is the integral sign, f(x) the integrand and dx shows the variable.

## 4.7 Standard formulae

| ∫ … dx | Result (+ c) |
| --- | --- |
| x^n (n ≠ −1) | x^(n + 1)/(n + 1) |
| 1/x | ln \|x\| |
| e^x | e^x |
| e^(ax) | e^(ax)/a |
| a^x | a^x/ln a |
| sin x | −cos x |
| cos x | sin x |
| sec^2 x | tan x |
| cosec^2 x | −cot x |
| sec x tan x | sec x |
| cosec x cot x | −cosec x |
| 1/(1 + x^2) | tan^−1 x |
| 1/√(1 − x^2) | sin^−1 x |
| 1/(x^2 + a^2) | (1/a) tan^−1(x/a) |
| 1/(x^2 − a^2) | (1/2a) ln \|(x − a)/(x + a)\| |
| 1/(a^2 − x^2) | (1/2a) ln \|(a + x)/(a − x)\| |

## 4.8 Rules of integration

1. ∫ k·f(x) dx = k ∫ f(x) dx (a constant comes out).
2. ∫ [f(x) ± g(x)] dx = ∫ f dx ± ∫ g dx.
3. There is **no** simple product rule: ∫ fg dx is not (∫f)(∫g). Products need substitution or integration by parts.

```text
(1) ∫ (3x^2 + 4x − 5) dx = x^3 + 2x^2 − 5x + c

(2) ∫ (x^2 + 1)^2/x^2 dx = ∫ (x^4 + 2x^2 + 1)/x^2 dx
    = ∫ (x^2 + 2 + x^(−2)) dx
    = x^3/3 + 2x − 1/x + c

(3) ∫ (e^x + 1/x + cos x) dx = e^x + ln|x| + sin x + c
```

## 4.9 Method of substitution

If part of the integrand is the derivative of another part, put that other part = t.

```text
(4) ∫ 2x/(x^2 + 1) dx
    t = x^2 + 1, dt = 2x dx
    = ∫ dt/t = ln t = ln(x^2 + 1) + c

(5) ∫ x e^(x^2) dx
    t = x^2, dt = 2x dx → x dx = dt/2
    = (1/2)∫ e^t dt = (1/2)e^(x^2) + c

(6) ∫ (ln x)/x dx
    t = ln x, dt = dx/x
    = ∫ t dt = (ln x)^2/2 + c

(7) ∫ (2x + 3)^5 dx
    t = 2x + 3, dx = dt/2
    = (1/2) t^6/6 = (2x + 3)^6/12 + c

(8) ∫ tan x dx = ∫ sin x/cos x dx
    t = cos x, dt = −sin x dx
    = −∫ dt/t = −ln|cos x| = ln|sec x| + c
```

Rule worth remembering: ∫ f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + c.

## 4.10 Method of partial fractions

Split the rational function (Unit 1) and integrate each piece.

```text
(9) ∫ dx/(x^2 − a^2)
    1/(x^2 − a^2) = (1/2a)[1/(x − a) − 1/(x + a)]
    check: (x + a − x + a)/(x^2 − a^2) = 2a/(x^2 − a^2) ✓
    = (1/2a)[ln|x − a| − ln|x + a|]
    = (1/2a) ln|(x − a)/(x + a)| + c

(10) ∫ (3x + 5)/((x + 2)(x − 1)) dx
     = ∫ [1/(3(x + 2)) + 8/(3(x − 1))] dx
     = (1/3) ln|x + 2| + (8/3) ln|x − 1| + c

(11) ∫ dx/((x − 1)(x − 2))
     1/((x − 1)(x − 2)) = −1/(x − 1) + 1/(x − 2)
     = ln|x − 2| − ln|x − 1| = ln|(x − 2)/(x − 1)| + c
```

## 4.11 Integration by parts

For a product of two functions u and v:

```text
∫ u·v dx = u ∫ v dx − ∫ [ u′ · ∫ v dx ] dx
```

Choose u (the first function) by **ILATE**: Inverse trigonometric, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential — whichever comes first in this list is u.

```text
(12) ∫ x e^x dx       u = x, v = e^x
     = x e^x − ∫ 1·e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c

(13) ∫ x sin x dx     u = x, v = sin x
     = x(−cos x) − ∫ 1·(−cos x) dx
     = −x cos x + sin x + c

(14) ∫ ln x dx = ∫ ln x · 1 dx    u = ln x, v = 1
     = x ln x − ∫ (1/x)·x dx = x ln x − x + c

(15) ∫ x ln x dx      u = ln x, v = x
     = (x^2/2) ln x − ∫ (1/x)(x^2/2) dx
     = (x^2/2) ln x − x^2/4 + c
```

Check any result by differentiating it: d/dx (x e^x − e^x) = x e^x + e^x − e^x = x e^x ✓.

## 4.12 Definite integrals

```text
∫ (from a to b) f(x) dx = [F(x)] from a to b = F(b) − F(a)
```

No constant c is needed. Properties: swapping the limits changes the sign; ∫ from a to a = 0.

```text
(16) ∫ (1 to 2) (5x^4 + 2x + 2) dx
     = [x^5 + x^2 + 2x] from 1 to 2
     = (32 + 4 + 4) − (1 + 1 + 2) = 40 − 4 = 36

(17) ∫ (0 to 1) x e^x dx = [x e^x − e^x] from 0 to 1
     = (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1

(18) ∫ (0 to π/2) sin x dx = [−cos x] = −0 + 1 = 1

(19) ∫ (0 to 1) dx/(1 + x^2) = [tan^−1 x] = π/4 − 0 = π/4
```

## 4.13 Applications of integration

**Area under a curve.** The area between y = f(x), the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b is ∫ (a to b) f(x) dx. Example: area under y = x^2 from 0 to 3 = [x^3/3] from 0 to 3 = 9 square units.

**Area under the plasma concentration–time curve (AUC).** AUC measures the total amount of drug that reached the blood and is used to compare bioavailability. For an IV bolus with C = C0 e^(−kt):

```text
AUC (0 to ∞) = ∫ C0 e^(−kt) dt = C0 [−e^(−kt)/k] from 0 to ∞
             = C0 (0 + 1/k) = C0/k
C0 = 20 µg/ml, k = 0.2 per h → AUC = 100 µg·h/ml
```

**Trapezoidal rule (from lab data).** Area of each strip = (C1 + C2)/2 × (t2 − t1); add the strips.

```text
t (h):     0    1    2    4
C (µg/ml): 10   8    6    4
strips: (10 + 8)/2 × 1 = 9
        (8 + 6)/2 × 1  = 7
        (6 + 4)/2 × 2  = 10
AUC (0 to 4 h) = 26 µg·h/ml
```

**Other uses:** amount of drug released from a rate equation, total amount excreted in urine, work done, and the integrated rate laws of kinetics.

## Remember

- Quadrant signs: I (+, +), II (−, +), III (−, −), IV (+, −).
- Distance = √[(x2 − x1)^2 + (y2 − y1)^2]; slope = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1) = tan θ.
- Parallel: m1 = m2; perpendicular: m1m2 = −1; ax + by + c = 0 has slope −a/b.
- y = mx + c; y − y1 = m(x − x1).
- ∫x^n dx = x^(n + 1)/(n + 1) + c; ∫dx/x = ln|x|; ∫e^(ax) = e^(ax)/a.
- Substitution: ∫ f′/f dx = ln|f|; partial fractions for rational functions; parts: ILATE.
- Definite integral = F(b) − F(a); AUC (IV bolus) = C0/k; trapezoids = (C1 + C2)/2 × Δt.

# Unit 5: Differential equations and Laplace transform

A **differential equation** links a quantity with its rate of change. Almost every equation in pharmacokinetics and chemical kinetics starts as one: "the rate of loss of drug is proportional to the amount present" is dX/dt = −kX. Solving it gives the familiar exponential curve. The **Laplace transform** is a tool that turns such equations into simple algebra, which is why it is used for multi-step models such as absorption followed by elimination.

## Part A: Differential equations

## 5.1 Basic definitions

- **Differential equation (DE):** an equation containing derivatives of a dependent variable with respect to an independent variable, e.g. dy/dx = 3x^2.
- **Ordinary DE:** only one independent variable (all in this syllabus).
- **Order:** the order of the highest derivative present.
- **Degree:** the power of the highest-order derivative, after the equation is made free of fractional powers (roots) of the derivatives.
- **General solution:** contains as many arbitrary constants as the order. **Particular solution:** constants found from given conditions (initial conditions).

| Equation | Order | Degree |
| --- | --- | --- |
| d²y/dx² + 3 dy/dx + 2y = 0 | 2 | 1 |
| (dy/dx)^3 + y = x | 1 | 3 |
| (d²y/dx²)^2 + (dy/dx)^3 = 0 | 2 | 2 |
| d³y/dx³ + y = sin x | 3 | 1 |
| y = x(dy/dx) + √(1 + (dy/dx)^2) | 1 | 2 |

For the last one, move x(dy/dx) across and square: (y − x·p)^2 = 1 + p^2, where p = dy/dx. The highest power of p is now 2, so the degree is 2.

## 5.2 Equations in separable form (variables separable)

If the equation can be written f(y) dy = g(x) dx, integrate both sides.

```text
(1) dy/dx = x/y
    y dy = x dx → y^2/2 = x^2/2 + c
    → y^2 − x^2 = C

(2) dy/dx = e^(x − y) = e^x · e^(−y)
    e^y dy = e^x dx → e^y = e^x + c

(3) (1 + x^2) dy = (1 + y^2) dx
    dy/(1 + y^2) = dx/(1 + x^2)
    tan^−1 y = tan^−1 x + c

(4) dy/dx = ky   (k constant)
    dy/y = k dx → ln y = kx + c
    → y = A e^(kx)   (A = e^c)
```

Example (4) is the growth/decay law used in Section 5.6.

## 5.3 Homogeneous equations

dy/dx = f(x, y)/g(x, y) is **homogeneous** if f and g are homogeneous functions of the same degree (every term has the same total power of x and y). Then dy/dx can be written as a function of y/x.

**Method:** put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. The variables then separate.

```text
(5) dy/dx = (x + y)/x
    y = vx: v + x dv/dx = 1 + v
    x dv/dx = 1 → dv = dx/x
    v = ln|x| + c → y = x ln|x| + cx

(6) dy/dx = (x^2 + y^2)/(2xy)
    y = vx: v + x dv/dx = (1 + v^2)/(2v)
    x dv/dx = (1 + v^2 − 2v^2)/(2v) = (1 − v^2)/(2v)
    2v dv/(1 − v^2) = dx/x
    −ln|1 − v^2| = ln|x| + c
    x(1 − v^2) = C → x(1 − y^2/x^2) = C
    → x^2 − y^2 = Cx
    Check: 2x − 2y y′ = C = (x^2 − y^2)/x
    → y′ = (x^2 + y^2)/(2xy) ✓
```

## 5.4 Linear differential equations

A first-order **linear** DE has the form

```text
dy/dx + P y = Q      (P, Q functions of x only)
Integrating factor (IF) = e^(∫P dx)
Solution: y × IF = ∫ (Q × IF) dx + c
```

```text
(7) dy/dx + y = e^x
    P = 1, IF = e^x
    y e^x = ∫ e^x · e^x dx = e^(2x)/2 + c
    y = e^x/2 + c e^(−x)
    Check: y′ + y = e^x/2 − c e^(−x) + e^x/2 + c e^(−x)
          = e^x ✓

(8) dy/dx + y/x = x^2
    P = 1/x, IF = e^(ln x) = x
    xy = ∫ x^3 dx = x^4/4 + c
    y = x^3/4 + c/x

(9) dy/dx − 2y = 4, y(0) = 1
    IF = e^(−2x)
    y e^(−2x) = ∫ 4e^(−2x) dx = −2e^(−2x) + c
    y = −2 + c e^(2x); y(0) = 1 → c = 3
    y = 3e^(2x) − 2
```

## 5.5 Exact equations

M dx + N dy = 0 (M, N functions of x and y) is **exact** if

```text
∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x
```

∂M/∂y (a **partial derivative**) means differentiate M with respect to y treating x as a constant; ∂N/∂x means differentiate N with respect to x treating y as a constant.

**Solution:** ∫ M dx (treat y as constant) + ∫ (terms of N not containing x) dy = c.

```text
(10) (2xy + 3) dx + (x^2 + 4y) dy = 0
     ∂M/∂y = 2x, ∂N/∂x = 2x → exact
     ∫ M dx = x^2 y + 3x
     terms of N without x: 4y → ∫ 4y dy = 2y^2
     Solution: x^2 y + 3x + 2y^2 = c

(11) (x^2 − ay) dx + (y^2 − ax) dy = 0
     ∂M/∂y = −a, ∂N/∂x = −a → exact
     ∫ M dx = x^3/3 − axy
     N terms without x: y^2 → y^3/3
     x^3/3 − axy + y^3/3 = c
     or x^3 + y^3 − 3axy = C
```

## 5.6 Application in solving pharmacokinetic and kinetic equations

**1. First-order elimination (IV bolus, one compartment).**

```text
dC/dt = −kC   (separable)
dC/C = −k dt → ln C = −kt + c
At t = 0, C = C0 → c = ln C0
C = C0 e^(−kt)
log C = log C0 − kt/2.303
Half-life: C = C0/2 → t½ = ln 2/k = 0.693/k

Example: k = 0.1155 per h, C0 = 40 µg/ml
t½ = 0.693/0.1155 = 6 h
After 12 h (two half-lives): C = 40 × 1/4 = 10 µg/ml
```

**2. Zero-order process.**

```text
dC/dt = −k0 → C = C0 − k0 t
t½ = C0/(2k0)
```

**3. Constant-rate IV infusion (linear DE).** Drug enters at a constant rate k0 (mg/h) and leaves by first-order elimination:

```text
dX/dt = k0 − kX  →  dX/dt + kX = k0
IF = e^(kt)
X e^(kt) = ∫ k0 e^(kt) dt = (k0/k) e^(kt) + c
X(0) = 0 → c = −k0/k
X = (k0/k)(1 − e^(−kt))
As t → ∞, X → k0/k (steady state)
Css = k0/(kV) = k0/CL

Example: k0 = 10 mg/h, k = 0.1 per h, V = 20 L
Xss = 100 mg, Css = 5 mg/L
At t = t½ = 6.93 h, X = 50 mg (half of steady state)
```

## Part B: Laplace transform

## 5.7 Definition

For a function f(t) defined for t ≥ 0, the **Laplace transform** is

```text
L{f(t)} = F(s) = ∫ (0 to ∞) e^(−st) f(t) dt
```

It changes a function of time t into a function of a new variable s. Its main power: **differentiation in t becomes multiplication by s**, so a DE becomes an algebraic equation.

**Deriving two results:**

```text
L{1} = ∫ (0 to ∞) e^(−st) dt = [−e^(−st)/s] (0 to ∞)
     = 0 + 1/s = 1/s      (s > 0)

L{e^(at)} = ∫ e^(−(s − a)t) dt = 1/(s − a)   (s > a)
```

## 5.8 Laplace transforms of elementary functions

| f(t) | F(s) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 1/s |
| t | 1/s^2 |
| t^n (n = 1, 2, 3 …) | n!/s^(n + 1) |
| e^(at) | 1/(s − a) |
| e^(−at) | 1/(s + a) |
| sin at | a/(s^2 + a^2) |
| cos at | s/(s^2 + a^2) |
| sinh at | a/(s^2 − a^2) |
| cosh at | s/(s^2 − a^2) |

## 5.9 Properties

| Property | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| Linearity | L{a f + b g} = a F(s) + b G(s) |
| First shifting | L{e^(at) f(t)} = F(s − a) |
| Change of scale | L{f(at)} = (1/a) F(s/a) |
| Multiplication by t | L{t f(t)} = −dF/ds |
| Derivative | L{f′(t)} = sF(s) − f(0) |
| Second derivative | L{f″(t)} = s^2 F(s) − s f(0) − f′(0) |

```text
(12) L{3t^2 + 2e^(−3t) − 4 sin 2t}
     = 3(2/s^3) + 2/(s + 3) − 4(2/(s^2 + 4))
     = 6/s^3 + 2/(s + 3) − 8/(s^2 + 4)

(13) L{e^(2t) sin 3t}: L{sin 3t} = 3/(s^2 + 9);
     replace s by s − 2 → 3/((s − 2)^2 + 9)

(14) L{t e^(−t)}: L{t} = 1/s^2 → 1/(s + 1)^2
```

## 5.10 Inverse Laplace transform

L^−1{F(s)} = f(t) means L{f(t)} = F(s). Read the table backwards, using partial fractions when needed.

```text
(15) L^−1{1/(s + 4)}      = e^(−4t)
(16) L^−1{5/(s^2 + 25)}   = sin 5t
(17) L^−1{s/(s^2 + 9)}    = cos 3t
(18) L^−1{1/s^3}          = t^2/2

(19) L^−1{1/((s + 1)(s + 2))}
     1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) = 1/(s + 1) − 1/(s + 2)
     = e^(−t) − e^(−2t)

(20) L^−1{(3s + 5)/((s + 2)(s − 1))}
     = L^−1{(1/3)/(s + 2) + (8/3)/(s − 1)}
     = (1/3)e^(−2t) + (8/3)e^t

(21) L^−1{(s + 3)/(s^2 + 4s + 13)}
     s^2 + 4s + 13 = (s + 2)^2 + 9
     (s + 3) = (s + 2) + 1
     = e^(−2t) cos 3t + (1/3) e^(−2t) sin 3t
```

## 5.11 Solving linear differential equations

**Steps:** (1) take the Laplace transform of both sides, using the derivative formulas and the initial values; (2) solve the algebra for Y(s); (3) split by partial fractions; (4) take the inverse transform.

```text
(22) y′ + 2y = 0, y(0) = 3
     sY − 3 + 2Y = 0 → Y = 3/(s + 2)
     y = 3e^(−2t)

(23) y′ + y = 1, y(0) = 0
     sY + Y = 1/s → Y = 1/(s(s + 1))
     = 1/s − 1/(s + 1)
     y = 1 − e^(−t)

(24) y″ − 3y′ + 2y = 0, y(0) = 0, y′(0) = 1
     (s^2 Y − 0 − 1) − 3(sY − 0) + 2Y = 0
     Y(s^2 − 3s + 2) = 1
     Y = 1/((s − 1)(s − 2)) = −1/(s − 1) + 1/(s − 2)
     y = e^(2t) − e^t
     Check: y(0) = 0; y′ = 2e^(2t) − e^t → y′(0) = 1 ✓
```

## 5.12 Application in chemical kinetics and pharmacokinetics

**1. IV bolus.** dX/dt = −kX, X(0) = D (the dose).

```text
sX̄ − D = −kX̄ → X̄ = D/(s + k) → X = D e^(−kt)
```

(X̄ is the Laplace transform of X.)

**2. Oral dose, one compartment, first-order absorption.** Xa = amount at the absorption site, X = amount in the body, F = fraction absorbed.

```text
dXa/dt = −ka Xa,          Xa(0) = F·D
dX/dt  = ka Xa − kX,      X(0)  = 0
Transform:
X̄a = F·D/(s + ka)
sX̄ = ka X̄a − kX̄ → X̄ = ka F D/((s + ka)(s + k))
Partial fractions:
1/((s + ka)(s + k)) = [1/(ka − k)] [1/(s + k) − 1/(s + ka)]
Inverse:
X = [ka F D/(ka − k)] (e^(−kt) − e^(−ka·t))
C = X/V
```

This is the **Bateman equation** that describes the rise and fall of blood levels after a tablet. The time of its peak is found in Unit 3.

**3. IV infusion.** dX/dt = k0 − kX, X(0) = 0.

```text
sX̄ = k0/s − kX̄ → X̄ = k0/(s(s + k))
= (k0/k)[1/s − 1/(s + k)]
X = (k0/k)(1 − e^(−kt))   (same answer as 5.6)
```

**4. Consecutive reactions A → B → C** (rate constants k1, k2) give the same algebra as the oral model: [B] = k1A0/(k2 − k1) × (e^(−k1 t) − e^(−k2 t)). Drug degradation through an intermediate follows this pattern.

## Remember

- Order = highest derivative; degree = its power after removing roots.
- Separable: f(y)dy = g(x)dx; homogeneous: y = vx; linear: IF = e^(∫P dx), y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + c.
- Exact if ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x; solution ∫M dx + ∫(N terms without x) dy = c.
- dC/dt = −kC → C = C0e^(−kt), t½ = 0.693/k; infusion → X = (k0/k)(1 − e^(−kt)).
- L{f} = ∫ (0 to ∞) e^(−st) f dt; L{1} = 1/s, L{t^n} = n!/s^(n + 1), L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a), L{sin at} = a/(s^2 + a^2), L{cos at} = s/(s^2 + a^2).
- L{f′} = sF − f(0); L{f″} = s^2F − s f(0) − f′(0); first shifting: e^(at) → s − a.
- Laplace method: transform → solve for Y → partial fractions → inverse.
